It sells through nine retail formats built on in-house labels (Metro, Mochi, Walkway) and international partner brands (Crocs, FitFlop, Foot Locker, FILA, New Era, Clarks), plus a multi-brand sports-performance format, MetroActiv. The Company does not manufacture: it follows a capital-light model based on outsourced manufacturing and long-standing vendor relationships, and reaches customers through its own stores, brand …

currentContext.strengths: Established brand recall built over decades around trusted in-house brands, with a high proportion of repeat customers contributing a significant share of revenue|Preferred partner for leading global brands seeking Indian entry — FitFlop, Crocs, Foot Locker, FILA, New Era and Clarks — on the strength of retail reach, consumer understanding and brand-building track record|One of India's largest speciality footwear retail networks, with over 1,000 stores spanning metro, Tier I, Tier II and Tier III markets|Diversified portfolio of owned, licensed and international brands across genders, occasions and price points, reducing dependence on any single category|Integrated omni-channel platform linking stores with brand websites, marketplaces and omni-channel fulfilment, supported by a dedicated Warehouse Management System and Order Management System|Scalable asset-light / capital-light model: outsourced manufacturing plus a Company-Owned Company-Operated retail model giving control over customer experience and merchandising|Robust sourcing and vendor ecosystem — more than 250 vendors dealt with over the last three fiscal years — supporting sourcing flexibility and faster response to fashion trends|Disciplined capital allocation with clear return thresholds on expansion, control over discounting and working capital, and a healthy balance sheet with strong cash generation|Machine-learning-based demand forecasting and inventory replenishment reducing stock-outs and stale inventory, with in-house AI agents under development|Promoter-led leadership combined with a professional management team with a proven execution record|Active intellectual-property protection framework, including enforcement actions and interim relief from the Hon'ble Bombay High Court protecting the 'METRO' trademarks
currentContext.strategies: Three-pronged next phase of store expansion: strengthen successful clusters by opening same-format stores at appropriate distances without materially cannibalising the existing network; backfill established cities with complementary formats where the market and customer are already understood; and enter newer cities to broaden reach.|In a new market, begin with Metro and progressively introduce formats such as Mochi, Crocs or Walkway as understanding of local demand deepens.|Grow with precision rather than pursue a predetermined store count — every opportunity evaluated against customer demand, site quality, rental economics and ability to generate sustainable returns, with financial discipline determining the pace and quality of expansion.|Add brands and formats only where they address a meaningful, unmet consumer need and where MBL's retail reach, local market understanding and operating capabilities can build that brand more effectively in India.|Scale the refined Walkway format for aspirational, value-conscious consumers, especially across Tier 2 markets (33 net store additions during FY 2025-26).|Phased rollout of Clarks: launched online and introduced the Cloudsteppers range through the Metro and Mochi network first, with wider assortment and exclusive stores to follow once the product range and supply chain stabilise.|Use MetroActiv's first three stores to test the sports-performance concept across different consumer markets, refine the assortment and strengthen the service model before scaling further.|Lean into premiumisation and casualisation, with sports and athleisure becoming everyday wardrobe categories addressed by MetroActiv, Foot Locker, FILA, New Era and Clarks.|Deploy data, AI and machine learning across merchandising, inventory planning and store expansion — demand forecasting, initial allocation and replenishment to improve availability and cut excess/ageing inventory; location intelligence on catchments, demographics and competition to guide site selection.|Strengthen omni-channel systems connecting brand websites, marketplaces, stores and omnichannel touchpoints, including warehouse and order-management capabilities.|Maintain financial discipline over growth: partnerships assessed against clear strategic and return criteria, capital allocated selectively, and no growth pursued at the expense of profitability.|Invest in distribution infrastructure, supply-chain capacity, talent, marketing and customer engagement to build the organisational readiness for a larger network and broader portfolio.|Build the leadership bench through structured programmes (Potential Manager Programme, Potential Area Manager Programme, Store Operations Management Trainee, Area Operations Management Trainee) and the partnership with BIMTECH.|Extend the footwear recovery ecosystem channelling discarded footwear towards recycling, co-processing and energy recovery, alongside water conservation and afforestation initiatives.
currentContext.expansion: Metro Brands' expansion is retail-footprint expansion rather than plant capex: it operates an asset-light model with outsourced manufacturing and undertakes no manufacturing activity of its own. During FY 2025-26 the Company opened 147 stores and closed 23, a net addition of 124, crossing the 1,000-store milestone and ending the year with 1,032 stores across 221 cities in 31 states and Union Territories, spanning the Metro, Mochi, Crocs, Walkway, Foot Locker, FitFlop, MetroActiv, FILA and New Era formats. Walkway was the strongest expansion of the year with 33 net store additions as the Company began scaling the refined value format for aspirational, value-conscious consumers, particularly across Tier 2 markets. The Company launched MetroActiv, a new multi-brand sports-performance and athleisure format, opening its first store in Indore followed by Dehradun and Jodhpur, and launched the dedicated e-commerce platform metroactiv.com; these three locations are described as a test of the concept across different consumer markets before scaling further. A strategic agreement with Clarks was entered in June 2025; the brand was launched on the Company's D2C platform and leading marketplaces and the Cloudsteppers women's range was distributed across the multi-brand outlet network, with the wider assortment and exclusive Clarks stores to be introduced only after the product range and supply chain stabilise. Foot Locker's presence in India was expanded, the FILA business was scaled through product assortment, sourcing, retail execution and distribution initiatives, and New Era's growth was accelerated alongside dedicated direct-to-consumer digital platforms. The next phase of expansion is described as three-pronged: strengthening successful clusters with same-format stores placed at distances that avoid material cannibalisation, backfilling established cities with complementary formats, and entering newer cities — typically beginning a new market with Metro and progressively adding Mochi, Crocs or Walkway. Each opportunity is evaluated against customer demand, site quality, rental economics and its ability to generate sustainable returns rather than against a predetermined store count. On the infrastructure side, the Company operated 2 warehouses and 1 office alongside its 1,032 showrooms; the BRSR notes that one warehouse facility was commissioned in April 2026 while one old warehouse facility was surrendered back to the developer, and the Chairman describes investment during the year in distribution infrastructure and supply-chain capacity. Digital and technology build-out continued, with e-commerce and omni-channel sales up 39% to Rs 361 crore (approximately 12.9% of total sales), AI and machine-learning-based demand forecasting, allocation and replenishment, and location-intelligence capabilities applied to site selection.
currentContext.mdna: India's consumption story — rising aspirations, increasing brand awareness, formalisation of retail and wider adoption of digital commerce — is reshaping consumer markets, visibly beyond the largest cities.|Premiumisation and casualisation are gaining ground and consumers increasingly move between formal, casual, comfort, fashion and performance categories, expecting one brand to serve several aspects of their lifestyle.|The Indian footwear industry, valued between US$ 17-18 billion in 2024, is projected to grow at a 10.1% CAGR during 2025-2033, with the organised sector expected to outpace the broader market.|India's branded Sports & Athleisure footwear market is projected to grow at a 13% CAGR between FY 2024-25 and FY 2044-45, positioning organised multi-brand footwear retailers to benefit.|Growth drivers cited for the organised segment: increasing demand for branded products, premiumisation, expansion of modern retail formats, deeper penetration into Tier II and Tier III cities and continued growth of omni-channel retailing.|Within FY 2025-26, revenue growth accelerated quarter by quarter (9% in Q1, 11% in Q2, 15% in Q3, 20% in Q4); the year began at a measured pace as an early monsoon affected customer movement in some key markets, after which footfalls improved on stronger festive and wedding-season demand and the positive impact of GST reductions on consumer sentiment.|Digital commerce is a growing driver — e-commerce and omni-channel sales rose 39% during the year to Rs 361 crore, contributing approximately 12.9% of total sales.|Rising disposable incomes, increasing urbanisation and continued premiumisation are expected to support consumer demand across discretionary spending categories.|Demographic advantage, rapid urbanisation and rising aspirations in emerging cities, plus greater digital penetration in Tier II and Tier III cities, are cited as long-term penetration opportunities.|Margin lever: the increasing consumer preference for higher-value products is expected to support margin expansion and improve profitability.|Headwinds flagged: intensifying competition from organised domestic brands, international players, digital-first retailers and e-commerce platforms pressuring pricing, customer acquisition and market share; volatility in sourcing costs and supply chains plus pricing pressure from increased online discounting; vendor concentration; rapidly changing fashion trends and shorter product life cycles risking inventory obsolescence; and counterfeiting/IP infringement.|Management states the next phase of retail will increasingly be shaped by data, automation and emerging technologies, and intends to remain aligned with that direction.

risks.note: The MD&A 'Threats' section states the Indian footwear industry continues to witness increasing competition from organised domestic brands, international players, digital-first retailers and e-commerce platforms, resulting in heightened pressure on pricing, customer acquisition and market share. Management's response is a diversified brand portfolio and family-oriented retail proposition, expansion of omni-channel presence across B2C and B2B marketplaces, and digitised loyalty programmes supported by customer data and analytics.

risks.risk: Volatility in sourcing costs and supply chains, and margin pressure from online discounting
risks.note: Flagged in the MD&A: disruptions in global supply chains, fluctuations in sourcing costs and pricing pressures arising from increased online discounting may impact product availability, inventory planning and profitability. Mitigation cited is prudent inventory management, diversified sourcing strategies, disciplined pricing, a calibrated promotional approach and controlled discounting across digital channels.

Explicitly named as 'Vendor Concentration Risk' in the MD&A: dependence on a limited number of suppliers and brand partners for certain product categories may expose the Company to supply disruptions, procurement challenges and constraints in product availability. It is structural for an asset-light retailer whose entire product supply is outsourced. Mitigation is a broader sourcing base and multiple vendor and strategic-partner relationships.

risks.risk: Changing consumer preferences and shorter fashion cycles driving inventory obsolescence
risks.note: The MD&A notes that rapidly evolving fashion trends, changing consumer expectations and shorter product life cycles demand continuous product innovation and agile merchandising, and that failure to respond may result in inventory obsolescence and reduced consumer relevance. Because the model carries owned inventory across a 1,032-store network, this is where a demand miss turns directly into markdowns.

The MD&A states the prevalence of counterfeits and unauthorised trademark use may adversely affect brand reputation, consumer confidence and legitimate sales. The Directors' Report confirms this is an active, not theoretical, exposure: multiple enforcement actions were undertaken during the year across physical and digital channels, with interim relief granted by the Hon'ble Bombay High Court in proceedings to protect the Company's 'METRO' trademarks against deceptively similar marks.

risks.risk: Single-business, single-country concentration in a discretionary category
risks.note: The BRSR describes the Company as a footwear specialty retailer with its retail and ecommerce presence across cities and towns in India — one business, one country. There is no product-line or geographic diversification to absorb a downturn in Indian discretionary consumption, and the MD&A itself frames the demand outlook in terms of 'consumer demand across discretionary spending categories'. The Cautionary Statement to the Management Discussion and Analysis reinforces the dependency, naming macroeconomic developments within the country and improvements in capital market conditions as key factors that could influence operations, with actual outcomes liable to differ from expectations.

risks.risk: Very high employee attrition in a service-execution-dependent retail model
risks.note: The BRSR turnover-rate table shows permanent-employee attrition of 51.48% in FY 2025-26 (49.36% male, 69.53% female), essentially unchanged from 51.47% in FY 2024-25 though improved from 67.78% in FY 2023-24. With 5,179 permanent and 1,675 other-than-permanent employees staffing a retail network where in-store service is the differentiator, this level of churn is a persistent drag on training cost, service consistency and store productivity — which is why the Directors' Report emphasises structured talent-pipeline programmes (the Potential Manager Programme, Potential Area Manager Programme, Store Operations Management Trainee and Area Operations Management Trainee programmes) and 67 training sessions across behavioural, functional, technical and compliance domains during the year.

risks.risk: High and rising volume of customer grievances
risks.note: The BRSR transparency table records 33,970 customer complaints filed during FY 2025-26, up from 28,639 in the previous year, alongside 991 complaints from employees and workers (1,150 previously) and 14 from shareholders. All complaints were noted as resolved during the year and none were pending at year-end, but the rising customer-complaint count against an expanding store and e-commerce base is a service-quality and brand-reputation watch item.

one-line thesis: Metro Brands defied discretionary slowdown with 15% consolidated revenue growth (crossing INR 800cr) driven by festive demand and GST pass-through, while EBITDA margins held firm at 33% despite gestation costs from new formats. The key pivot is the measured slowdown in Foot Locker expansion due to BIS regulatory delays, offset by the successful launch of the tier-2 focused 'MetroActiv' concept and sustained double-digit volume growth.
financial scorecard: Revenue: INR 811cr (+15% YoY, first time >INR 800cr); EBITDA: INR 268cr (+18% YoY), Margin 33% (flat YoY); PAT: INR 129cr (+33% YoY, normalized for one-off tax charge in prior year); Order Book: N/A (Retail); Net Debt: Net Cash position (Special dividend paid in Q4FY25 reduced treasury income). One-offs: INR 3.3cr accrual for proposed Labour Code dampened PAT; IndAS 116 notional interest cost ~INR 39-40cr for 9MFY26.
guidance: Revenue CAGR ~15% (mid-high single digit SSG + 10% from new stores + annualization); EBITDA Margin ~33%; Store Openings: >100 in FY26, Foot Locker expansion now 'measured' pending BIS resolution (expected Q2FY27); Capex: Continued investment in new formats (MetroActiv, Foot Locker) and store fit-outs.
order book & pipeline: N/A - Retail business model relies on inventory turnover rather than order book; Inventory at INR 785cr+ (slight seasonal buildup in Q3, deemed healthy).
segment / subsidiary detail: Digital commerce grew 24% YoY (12% of total revenue); Premium segment (>INR 3,000) is 55% of mix; 'Other' revenue segment saw slight increase to ~2% due to decimal adjustments/no material change; Shoe Depot (outlet) format now 7 stores, replacing fragmented outlet strategy for better rental economics.
growth verticals / optionality: MetroActiv expansion into Tier 2/3 cities (Indore, Jodhpur); FILA business turnaround post-BIS/component sourcing hurdles; Walkway benefit from GST cuts on sub-INR 1,000 footwear; Omni-channel penetration in non-metro zip codes.
margins & cost dynamics: Gross Margin guided 55-58%; New formats (Foot Locker/MetroActiv) currently have lower incoming margins (90% third-party brands) and higher marketing/fit-out costs creating temporary EBITDA drag; ASP up 2.5-3%, Volume growth ~12% in Q3.
capex / expansion: Significant opex/capex in new store fit-outs (especially large format Foot Locker); Not capital constrained; Focus on profitability-adjusted expansion rather than fixed store count targets.
capital allocation: Special dividend paid in Q4FY25 reduced investable surplus; Future allocation towards organic store expansion and format refinement; No M&A mentioned.
risks & watch-items: BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) certification delays for imported athletic brands (Foot Locker/FILA) pushing resolution to Q2FY27; Regulatory uncertainty on Labour Code accruals; Discretionary consumption slowdown in non-festive quarters; Inventory buildup if seasonal demand misaligned.
management quality / tone: Confident on defying sector slowdown; Pragmatic on regulatory headwinds (BIS); Disciplined on capital allocation (profitability over blind expansion); Transparent on accounting impacts (IndAS, GST).
non-obvious takeaways: Revenue per sq ft appears 'flat' only because denominator includes full sq footage of new stores opened late in quarter; GST benefit is fully passed to consumers (3-4% lower effective price), driving volume rather than margin expansion; Shoe Depot format is a real estate arbitrage play (consolidating 3 small outlets into 1 large low-rent space) rather than just inventory liquidation.
challenges → beneficiaries & losers:
| Challenge | Beneficiary/Loser | Dir | Conviction | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BIS norms delaying import of premium athletic inventory, capping Foot Locker/FILA growth | Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail Ltd (ABFRL) | loser | Med | ABFRL's partnership with Forever 21 and other global brands faces similar import/regulatory scrutiny; Metro's delay highlights sector-wide friction for global athletic brands in India. |
| GST rate rationalization benefits value segment disproportionately | Metro Brands Limited | beneficiary | High | Direct pass-through of GST cuts (especially <INR 1,000 range) drives volume growth in Walkway/Metro Mochi, outperforming peers with less exposure to value footwear. |
| Shift to asset-light outlet model via Shoe Depot improves rental economics | Metro Brands Limited | beneficiary | Med | Consolidating outlet inventory into fewer, larger low-rent locations improves operating leverage compared to traditional mall-based outlet stores. |

themes.title: Quick-commerce, omnichannel & retail expansion
themes.need: Quick-commerce and value retail are the structural growth engine, and Q1FY27 rewrote the unit-economics model. ETERNAL raised Blinkit's steady-state margin from a 5-6% range to ~6% and set a first-ever 4% GAAP EBIT margin target (after ESOP and depreciation) while capex per store went from INR 1cr to INR 2.5cr (+150%) with NOV/store/day up only 60% and net working capital improving 18 to 14 days - so margin can now drift DOWN while ROCE improves. Growth also decoupled from spend: Blinkit orders +21% QoQ with MTUs above 30mn achieved on LOWER marketing spend and fewer store adds, and management called Q1 the peak of competitive intensity to date. VMM did INR 3,727cr (+18.7%) on 10% SSSG with gross margin up to 28.7% driven by lower promotional spend rather than price hikes, validated a small-format store at the same revenue/sq ft and 'pretty much the same' ROCE as large format (a ~3,000-store national opportunity), and found 20% of its quick-commerce customers had never shopped a Vishal store. SHOPERSTOP swung PAT positive (+INR 5cr vs -INR 4cr) and raised FY27 LFL guidance from 5% to ~6%; ARVINDFASN lifted gross margin 90bps to 56.7% on full-price sell-through with direct channels now 62% of sales; MEESHO cut cost per delivered order ~INR 1 QoQ despite the May fuel hike. DMART/V2RETAIL/PATELRMART on value retail; TRENT-tier branded retail via ABFRL/METROBRAND/BATAINDIA/REDTAPE.
themes.driver: Blinkit dark-store rollout at the new INR 2.5cr/store capex against the 4% GAAP EBIT target; VMM small-format expansion; festive/quick-commerce GMV. Watch ARVINDFASN's SS27 sourcing lock (next 45-60 days) - if war-inflated input costs hold, apparel pricing corrects.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Metro Brands Limited is one of India's largest speciality footwear and lifestyle retailers, running a predominantly Company-Owned Company-Operated network of 1,032 stores across nine differentiated formats spanning value, mid and premium price points.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Metro Brands is a footwear specialty retailer selling fashion footwear, bags and accessories for men, women and children across the economy, mid-range and premium segments. It sells through nine retail formats built on in-house labels (Metro, Mochi, Walkway) and international partner brands (Crocs, FitFlop, Foot Locker, FILA, New Era, Clarks), plus a multi-brand sports-performance format, MetroActiv. The Company does not manufacture: it follows a capital-light model based on outsourced manufacturing and long-standing vendor relationships, and reaches customers through its own stores, brand websites and e-commerce marketplaces.

segment_detail.title: Segment / subsidiary detail
segment_detail.body: Digital commerce grew 24% YoY (12% of total revenue); Premium segment (>INR 3,000) is 55% of mix; 'Other' revenue segment saw slight increase to ~2% due to decimal adjustments/no material change; Shoe Depot (outlet) format now 7 stores, replacing fragmented outlet strategy for better rental economics.

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **In-house brands / formats:** Metro, Mochi, Walkway
- **Third-party / partner brands:** Crocs, FitFlop, FILA, New Era, Foot Locker, Clarks
- **Multi-brand sports & athleisure format (MetroActiv):** Nike, adidas, Puma, ASICS, Skechers, New Balance, FILA, New Era
- **Product categories:** Men's footwear, Women's footwear, Kids' footwear, Unisex footwear, Bags, Clutches, Wallets, Belts, Foot care, Shoe care

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- India only — retail and e-commerce presence across metropolitan, Tier I, Tier II and Tier III cities
- 221 cities across 31 states and Union Territories
- Economy, mid-range and premium consumer segments; family footwear (men, women, children)
- High street, mall and airport store locations
- Digital: own brand websites, e-commerce marketplaces and quick-commerce platforms such as Zepto and Blinkit
- Exports negligible — 0.16% of total turnover; no international offices

order_book.title: Order book & pipeline
order_book.body: N/A - Retail business model relies on inventory turnover rather than order book; Inventory at INR 785cr+ (slight seasonal buildup in Q3, deemed healthy).

guidance.title: Guidance
guidance.body: Revenue CAGR ~15% (mid-high single digit SSG + 10% from new stores + annualization); EBITDA Margin ~33%; Store Openings: >100 in FY26, Foot Locker expansion now 'measured' pending BIS resolution (expected Q2FY27); Capex: Continued investment in new formats (MetroActiv, Foot Locker) and store fit-outs.

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body: MetroActiv expansion into Tier 2/3 cities (Indore, Jodhpur); FILA business turnaround post-BIS/component sourcing hurdles; Walkway benefit from GST cuts on sub-INR 1,000 footwear; Omni-channel penetration in non-metro zip codes.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India's consumption story — rising aspirations, increasing brand awareness, formalisation of retail and wider adoption of digital commerce — is reshaping consumer markets, visibly beyond the largest cities.
- Premiumisation and casualisation are gaining ground and consumers increasingly move between formal, casual, comfort, fashion and performance categories, expecting one brand to serve several aspects of their lifestyle.
- The Indian footwear industry, valued between US$ 17-18 billion in 2024, is projected to grow at a 10.1% CAGR during 2025-2033, with the organised sector expected to outpace the broader market.
- India's branded Sports & Athleisure footwear market is projected to grow at a 13% CAGR between FY 2024-25 and FY 2044-45, positioning organised multi-brand footwear retailers to benefit.
- Growth drivers cited for the organised segment: increasing demand for branded products, premiumisation, expansion of modern retail formats, deeper penetration into Tier II and Tier III cities and continued growth of omni-channel retailing.
- Within FY 2025-26, revenue growth accelerated quarter by quarter (9% in Q1, 11% in Q2, 15% in Q3, 20% in Q4); the year began at a measured pace as an early monsoon affected customer movement in some key markets, after which footfalls improved on stronger festive and wedding-season demand and the positive impact of GST reductions on consumer sentiment.
- Digital commerce is a growing driver — e-commerce and omni-channel sales rose 39% during the year to Rs 361 crore, contributing approximately 12.9% of total sales.
- Rising disposable incomes, increasing urbanisation and continued premiumisation are expected to support consumer demand across discretionary spending categories.
- Demographic advantage, rapid urbanisation and rising aspirations in emerging cities, plus greater digital penetration in Tier II and Tier III cities, are cited as long-term penetration opportunities.
- Margin lever: the increasing consumer preference for higher-value products is expected to support margin expansion and improve profitability.
- Headwinds flagged: intensifying competition from organised domestic brands, international players, digital-first retailers and e-commerce platforms pressuring pricing, customer acquisition and market share; volatility in sourcing costs and supply chains plus pricing pressure from increased online discounting; vendor concentration; rapidly changing fashion trends and shorter product life cycles risking inventory obsolescence; and counterfeiting/IP infringement.
- Management states the next phase of retail will increasingly be shaped by data, automation and emerging technologies, and intends to remain aligned with that direction.

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: Gross Margin guided 55-58%; New formats (Foot Locker/MetroActiv) currently have lower incoming margins (90% third-party brands) and higher marketing/fit-out costs creating temporary EBITDA drag; ASP up 2.5-3%, Volume growth ~12% in Q3.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Special dividend paid in Q4FY25 reduced investable surplus; Future allocation towards organic store expansion and format refinement; No M&A mentioned.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Metro Brands' expansion is retail-footprint expansion rather than plant capex: it operates an asset-light model with outsourced manufacturing and undertakes no manufacturing activity of its own. During FY 2025-26 the Company opened 147 stores and closed 23, a net addition of 124, crossing the 1,000-store milestone and ending the year with 1,032 stores across 221 cities in 31 states and Union Territories, spanning the Metro, Mochi, Crocs, Walkway, Foot Locker, FitFlop, MetroActiv, FILA and New Era formats. Walkway was the strongest expansion of the year with 33 net store additions as the Company began scaling the refined value format for aspirational, value-conscious consumers, particularly across Tier 2 markets. The Company launched MetroActiv, a new multi-brand sports-performance and athleisure format, opening its first store in Indore followed by Dehradun and Jodhpur, and launched the dedicated e-commerce platform metroactiv.com; these three locations are described as a test of the concept across different consumer markets before scaling further. A strategic agreement with Clarks was entered in June 2025; the brand was launched on the Company's D2C platform and leading marketplaces and the Cloudsteppers women's range was distributed across the multi-brand outlet network, with the wider assortment and exclusive Clarks stores to be introduced only after the product range and supply chain stabilise. Foot Locker's presence in India was expanded, the FILA business was scaled through product assortment, sourcing, retail execution and distribution initiatives, and New Era's growth was accelerated alongside dedicated direct-to-consumer digital platforms. The next phase of expansion is described as three-pronged: strengthening successful clusters with same-format stores placed at distances that avoid material cannibalisation, backfilling established cities with complementary formats, and entering newer cities — typically beginning a new market with Metro and progressively adding Mochi, Crocs or Walkway. Each opportunity is evaluated against customer demand, site quality, rental economics and its ability to generate sustainable returns rather than against a predetermined store count. On the infrastructure side, the Company operated 2 warehouses and 1 office alongside its 1,032 showrooms; the BRSR notes that one warehouse facility was commissioned in April 2026 while one old warehouse facility was surrendered back to the developer, and the Chairman describes investment during the year in distribution infrastructure and supply-chain capacity. Digital and technology build-out continued, with e-commerce and omni-channel sales up 39% to Rs 361 crore (approximately 12.9% of total sales), AI and machine-learning-based demand forecasting, allocation and replenishment, and location-intelligence capabilities applied to site selection.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Confident on defying sector slowdown; Pragmatic on regulatory headwinds (BIS); Disciplined on capital allocation (profitability over blind expansion); Transparent on accounting impacts (IndAS, GST).

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Established brand recall built over decades around trusted in-house brands, with a high proportion of repeat customers contributing a significant share of revenue
- Preferred partner for leading global brands seeking Indian entry — FitFlop, Crocs, Foot Locker, FILA, New Era and Clarks — on the strength of retail reach, consumer understanding and brand-building track record
- One of India's largest speciality footwear retail networks, with over 1,000 stores spanning metro, Tier I, Tier II and Tier III markets
- Diversified portfolio of owned, licensed and international brands across genders, occasions and price points, reducing dependence on any single category
- Integrated omni-channel platform linking stores with brand websites, marketplaces and omni-channel fulfilment, supported by a dedicated Warehouse Management System and Order Management System
- Scalable asset-light / capital-light model: outsourced manufacturing plus a Company-Owned Company-Operated retail model giving control over customer experience and merchandising
- Robust sourcing and vendor ecosystem — more than 250 vendors dealt with over the last three fiscal years — supporting sourcing flexibility and faster response to fashion trends
- Disciplined capital allocation with clear return thresholds on expansion, control over discounting and working capital, and a healthy balance sheet with strong cash generation
- Machine-learning-based demand forecasting and inventory replenishment reducing stock-outs and stale inventory, with in-house AI agents under development
- Promoter-led leadership combined with a professional management team with a proven execution record
- Active intellectual-property protection framework, including enforcement actions and interim relief from the Hon'ble Bombay High Court protecting the 'METRO' trademarks

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) certification delays for imported athletic brands (Foot Locker/FILA) pushing resolution to Q2FY27; Regulatory uncertainty on Labour Code accruals; Discretionary consumption slowdown in non-festive quarters; Inventory buildup if seasonal demand misaligned.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Revenue per sq ft appears 'flat' only because denominator includes full sq footage of new stores opened late in quarter; GST benefit is fully passed to consumers (3-4% lower effective price), driving volume rather than margin expansion; Shoe Depot format is a real estate arbitrage play (consolidating 3 small outlets into 1 large low-rent space) rather than just inventory liquidation.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Three-pronged next phase of store expansion: strengthen successful clusters by opening same-format stores at appropriate distances without materially cannibalising the existing network; backfill established cities with complementary formats where the market and customer are already understood; and enter newer cities to broaden reach.
- In a new market, begin with Metro and progressively introduce formats such as Mochi, Crocs or Walkway as understanding of local demand deepens.
- Grow with precision rather than pursue a predetermined store count — every opportunity evaluated against customer …

challenges.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers
challenges.body:
| Challenge | Beneficiary/Loser | Dir | Conviction | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BIS norms delaying import of premium athletic inventory, capping Foot Locker/FILA growth | Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail Ltd (ABFRL) | loser | Med | ABFRL's partnership with Forever 21 and other global brands faces similar import/regulatory scrutiny; Metro's delay highlights sector-wide friction for global athletic brands in India. |
| GST rate rationalization benefits value segment disproportionately | Metro Brands Limited | beneficiary | High | Direct pass-through of GST cuts (especially <INR 1,000 range) drives volume growth in Walkway/Metro Mochi, outperforming peers with less exposure to value footwear. |
| Shift to asset-light outlet model via Shoe Depot improves rental economics | Metro Brands Limited | beneficiary | Med | Consolidating outlet inventory into fewer, larger low-rent locations improves operating leverage compared to traditional mall-based outlet stores. |

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Acquisition] In 2022 the company acquired Cravatex Brands Ltd, gaining an exclusive license for Fila and ownership of the sportswear brand Proline.
- [Regulation - BIS] BIS implementation challenges faced by select external brands have impacted supply chain readiness (cautious approach to new Foot Locker and MetroActiv store expansion), and BIS related concerns drove the company to start local manufacturing of Fila footwear in India.
- [Milestones] The journey slide records: 2021 listed on BSE, NSE and hit 600 stores; 2023 strategic partnership with Foot Locker, hits 800 stores and market cap of $4B, crossed gross sales of Rs. 2500 crore; 2026 hits 1000 stores and crossed gross sales of Rs. 3000 crore. Note the deck's own label here is "gross sales", not revenue from operations.
- [Demand commentary] Q1 FY27 growth was "led by wedding season demand and improving sentiments from mid-June '26", while "April and May were relatively muted, weighed down by the US-Iran conflict overhang and a shift in marriage dates linked to Adhik Maas starting 17th May '26".
- [Management/Board] Rafique A. Malik is Chairman (associated with the Company since Jan 19, 1977), Farah Malik Bhanji is Managing Director, Nissan Joseph is Chief Executive Officer (previously with Payless Shoes, Hickory Brands, Crocs, MAP Active & Planet Sports), Kaushal Khodidas Parekh is CFO and Mohit Dhanjal is COO; independent directors include Bhaskar Bhat (ex-MD Titan), Radhika Dilip Piramal (ex-MD & CEO VIP Industries), Mithun Padam Sacheti (founder/ex-CEO CaratLane), Arvind Kumar Singhal (Technopak) and Vikas Vijaykumar Khemani, with Utpal Hemendra Sheth as Non-Executive (Nominee) Director.
